flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Wild Prairie Rose
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full entry.
flowers.description: North Dakota's state flower — a low-growing wild rose of the northern prairies with bright pink five-petaled flowers.

flowers.name: Wild Prairie Rose
flowers.wildlife: Native bee forage. Red hips persist through winter feeding grouse, pheasant, and songbirds. Dense thickets shelter ground-nesting birds.
flowers.description: North Dakota's state flower — a compact wild rose rarely exceeding 2 feet, with fragrant bright pink flowers and bright red hips. Spreads by rhizomes to form dense colonies. Among the most cold-hardy roses on earth, surviving temperatures of -40°F. Hips are exceptionally high in vitamin C.

flowers.name: Purple Coneflower
flowers.habitat: Dry prairies, rocky slopes, open grassland
flowers.wildlife: Major native bee and butterfly nectar plant. Goldfinches eat seeds directly from cones through winter.
flowers.description: The narrow-leaved coneflower native to the northern Great Plains — smaller and more drought-tolerant than its eastern cousin. The most historically significant medicinal plant of northern Plains tribes, used for pain, infections, and snake bite. Extremely deep taproot allows survival through severe drought.

flowers.name: Pasqueflower
flowers.wildlife: Critical first spring bee forage — often the first flower of the year on the northern plains.
flowers.description: The first wildflower of spring on the northern prairie — silky lavender blooms emerge through snow before any leaves appear. Covered in fine silver hairs that insulate against late freezes. The feathery seed plumes persist beautifully into summer. South Dakota's state flower. Among the most dramatic signs of spring's arrival.

flowers.name: Prairie Blazingstar
flowers.wildlife: One of the top monarch butterfly nectar plants. Major native bee forage. Hummingbirds visit during migration.
flowers.description: Tall spikes of brilliant magenta-purple flowers opening from top to bottom (unusual — most flowers open from bottom up). A spectacular midsummer prairie showpiece. One of the most important Monarch butterfly nectar sources during fall migration across the Great Plains.

flowers.name: Black-Eyed Susan
flowers.wildlife: Major pollinator nectar plant. Seeds eaten by goldfinches and sparrows through winter.
flowers.description: The quintessential prairie wildflower — golden yellow ray petals around a dark brown cone. Blooms for months through summer heat. Self-seeds freely in disturbed ground and roadsides. One of the most ecologically valuable wildflowers, supporting enormous diversity of pollinators.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Pasqueflower
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full entry.
flowers.description: South Dakota's state flower — the pasqueflower, first bloom of spring on the northern plains, covered in protective silver hairs.

flowers.name: Pasqueflower
flowers.habitat: Dry hilltops, sandy ridges, open prairie
flowers.wildlife: Critical first spring bee forage. Feathery seed plumes wind-dispersed across prairie.
flowers.description: South Dakota's beloved state flower — silky lavender blooms push through late-season snow before any leaves appear. The entire plant is covered in protective silver hairs. Blooms for only 2-3 weeks but produces spectacular feathery seed plumes that last months. A true symbol of the Great Plains spring.

flowers.name: Prairie Coneflower
flowers.wildlife: Native bee forage. Seeds eaten by birds. Drought tolerant.
flowers.description: Distinctive prairie wildflower with drooping yellow ray petals around a tall thimble-shaped brown cone. Also called Mexican Hat for its sombrero-like shape. Incredibly drought tolerant — thrives in the harshest South Dakota summers. Naturalizes freely along roadsides. Long blooming season.

flowers.name: Wild Bergamot
flowers.wildlife: Exceptional pollinator plant — supports hummingbirds, 20+ bee species, and dozens of butterfly and moth species.
flowers.description: Rounded lavender-pink flower heads on aromatic stems with oregano-scented leaves. One of the finest native perennials for the Great Plains — blooms for months, gradually spreads, and supports extraordinary pollinator diversity. Dried leaves make a pleasant wild oregano tea.

flowers.name: Leadplant
flowers.habitat: Dry prairies, rocky hillsides, open woodland
flowers.wildlife: Host for many rare butterflies including the Dogface Sulphur and Eastern Tailed Blue. Nitrogen fixer. Major bee forage.
flowers.description: A sprawling prairie shrub covered in silver-grey woolly leaves with small blue-purple flower spikes bearing bright orange anthers. An indicator of high-quality native prairie — where leadplant grows, the prairie is intact. Nitrogen-fixing root system. Used as 'prairie tea' by Plains tribes.

flowers.name: Maximilian Sunflower
flowers.wildlife: Major late-season bee and butterfly forage. Seeds critical for migrating birds. Goldfinches and sparrows overwinter on seed heads.
flowers.description: The great late-season sunflower of the northern plains — tall clump-forming plants covered in golden flowers in late summer when most prairie plants have finished. Essential for fall-migrating Monarchs and birds. Spreads by rhizomes to form large colonies. Incredibly drought tolerant.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Goldenrod
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full entry.
flowers.description: Nebraska's state flower — goldenrod, the ecological powerhouse of the prairie supporting 100+ insect species.

flowers.name: Goldenrod (Canada)
flowers.wildlife: Supports 100+ bee species, 20+ butterfly species, and 100+ moth caterpillar species. Essential for fall migrating Monarchs. Goldfinches eat seeds.
flowers.description: Nebraska's state flower and one of North America's most ecologically valuable plants. Arching plumes of tiny yellow flowers in late summer and fall — exactly when most other plants have finished. Incorrectly blamed for hay fever (ragweed is the culprit). An extraordinary ecological powerhouse.

flowers.name: Sand Phlox
flowers.habitat: Sand prairies, sandy woodland edges, dunes
flowers.wildlife: Early butterfly and bee forage. Spreads to form weed-suppressing groundcover.
flowers.description: Low spreading mats of lavender to white flowers with deeply notched petals — specific to the sandy prairies and dunes of the central Great Plains. Nebraska's Sandhills region hosts some of the finest populations. Spreads slowly to create a carpet of spring color. The notched petals are a distinctive characteristic.

flowers.name: Prairie Smoke
flowers.habitat: Dry prairies, rocky slopes, open ridges
flowers.wildlife: Early bee forage. Wind-dispersed feathery plumes are highly effective.
flowers.description: Three nodding pink-red bell-shaped flowers per stem transform into wispy pink-purple plumes as seeds develop — creating the effect of smoke rising from the prairie. One of the most distinctive and beautiful native plants for texture and movement. Thrives in the harsh conditions of the Nebraska plains.

flowers.name: Purple Prairie Clover
flowers.wildlife: Major native bee forage — specialist bees collect pollen exclusively from prairie clovers. Host for dogface butterfly. Nitrogen fixer.
flowers.description: Slender wands of vibrant magenta flowers opening in a ring that moves upward around a cylindrical head. The most striking of the prairie clovers. Nitrogen-fixing root system improves soil. An indicator of high-quality native prairie. Grazed by bison and deer.

flowers.name: Bison Plum (Ground Plum)
flowers.habitat: Dry prairies, rocky ridges, clay hills
flowers.wildlife: Native bee forage. Plum-like fruits eaten by many prairie animals. Nitrogen fixer.
flowers.description: Low-growing native milkvetch with purple pea flowers producing remarkable round plum-like pods that were eaten raw by Plains peoples — sweet and crisp when green. One of the most important wild foods of the Great Plains. Scattered across Nebraska's loess hills and clay prairies.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Sunflower
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full entry.
flowers.description: Kansas's state flower and the most iconic prairie wildflower — the common sunflower, ancestor of all domestic sunflowers, covering Kansas roadsides and fields in gold.

flowers.name: Common Sunflower
flowers.habitat: Prairies, roadsides, disturbed ground, field edges
flowers.wildlife: Seeds are among the most important food sources for birds — over 40 species eat sunflower seeds. Major bee forage. Orioles, finches, and grosbeaks depend on them during migration.
flowers.description: The wild ancestor of all cultivated sunflowers — native to Kansas and the southern plains. Plants vary from 3-12 feet with single or branched stems. Turns roadsides gold in late summer. The commercial sunflower industry began in Kansas. Seeds rich in oil and protein. One of the most important native food plants.

flowers.name: Compass Plant
flowers.habitat: Tallgrass prairie, clay hills, undisturbed grassland
flowers.wildlife: Supports specialist Silphium bees. Seeds eaten by goldfinches and songbirds. Deep roots indicate undisturbed prairie.
flowers.description: A spectacular 8-foot prairie giant with deeply cut rough leaves that orient north-south to minimize sun exposure (hence 'compass plant'). Yellow daisy flowers high on stiff stems. A keystone species of Kansas's remaining tallgrass prairie — its presence indicates soil that has never been plowed. Deep 15-foot taproot.

flowers.name: Prairie Blazingstar
flowers.wildlife: One of the top Monarch butterfly nectar plants. Major bee forage during peak migration.
flowers.description: Tall magenta spikes that light up the tallgrass prairie in midsummer. Critical for Monarch butterflies during their fall migration — the milkweed of nectar plants. Flowers open top to bottom (unusual). An iconic species of the Kansas Flint Hills — America's largest remaining tallgrass prairie.

flowers.name: Prairie Larkspur
flowers.habitat: Dry prairies, rocky slopes, open woodland
flowers.wildlife: Hummingbird nectar plant. Early bee forage.
flowers.description: Spikes of brilliant blue-violet flowers on slender stems across dry Kansas prairies in late spring. One of the most beautiful native wildflowers of the southern plains. Blooms briefly but brilliantly. All parts are toxic if eaten — keeps livestock from overgrazing prairie remnants.

flowers.name: Wild Blue Indigo
flowers.wildlife: Host for Wild Indigo Duskywing and Clouded Sulphur butterflies. Major bumblebee forage. Nitrogen-fixing root system.
flowers.description: Imposing blue-violet pea flowers on a substantial 4-foot plant with blue-green leaves. Extremely long-lived — individual plants in Kansas prairie remnants may be a century old. Black inflated seed pods rattle in winter. An important cultural plant used as a blue dye by many indigenous peoples.

flowers.name: ★ State Flower: Oklahoma Rose (Mistletoe)
flowers.wildlife: State symbol — see full entry.
flowers.description: Oklahoma's state flower — mistletoe, an unusual choice celebrating the parasitic plant that adorns the state's oak trees.

flowers.name: Indian Blanket (Firewheel)
flowers.wildlife: Major native bee and butterfly nectar. Goldfinches eat seeds. Drought tolerant.
flowers.description: Brilliant red and yellow bicolored daisy flowers that carpet Oklahoma roadsides in summer — named for their resemblance to Native American blankets. State wildflower of Oklahoma. Incredibly heat and drought tolerant. Blooms for months without supplemental water. Self-seeds prolifically.

flowers.name: Prairie Verbena
flowers.wildlife: Major butterfly nectar plant — dozens of species including fritillaries, swallowtails, and skippers. Drought tolerant groundcover.
flowers.description: Low spreading mats of lavender-purple verbena flowers blooming from early spring through late fall across Oklahoma's dry prairies. One of the longest-blooming native wildflowers. Creates weed-suppressing groundcover. Essential butterfly nectar source. Thrives in full sun and rocky soil.

flowers.name: Winecup
flowers.wildlife: Native bee nectar. Deep taproot survives Oklahoma's extreme summer heat.
flowers.description: Magenta-wine cup-shaped flowers on spreading low stems. Blooms profusely through spring, then dies back to a deep taproot to survive Oklahoma's brutal summer heat. One of the most drought-tolerant native wildflowers. Reappears reliably each spring. Creates stunning groundcover when established.

flowers.name: Plains Wild Indigo
flowers.habitat: Dry prairies, sandy soil, open woodland
flowers.wildlife: Host for Wild Indigo Duskywing butterfly. Early bee forage. Nitrogen fixer.
flowers.description: Pale cream-yellow pea flowers on a low-growing sprawling plant specific to the southern plains. One of the first wildflowers of spring in Oklahoma. Less common than its blue cousin but equally beautiful. The inflated black seed pods are striking in fall. Long-lived with a deep nitrogen-fixing taproot.

flowers.name: Cardinal Flower
flowers.habitat: Stream banks, wet meadows, moist woodland
flowers.wildlife: The most important hummingbird nectar plant in Oklahoma. Ruby-throated hummingbirds are the primary pollinator.
flowers.description: Brilliant scarlet spikes along Oklahoma's creek and river banks. The crimson color evolved specifically for hummingbird pollination — bees cannot see red well. One of the most spectacular native wildflowers. Spreads by self-seeding near water. Hummingbirds probe each flower for nectar.
